policy_title: Reduce Net Migration and Reform the Immigration System
stated: Labour will reduce net migration by reforming the points-based immigration system with appropriate visa restrictions and linking immigration to skills policy. They will bar employers who abuse the visa system or flout employment law from hiring workers from abroad. The Migration Advisory Committee will be strengthened, and workforce and training plans introduced for sectors reliant on overseas workers, ending long-term reliance on immigration shortage lists.

source.quote: So, Labour will reduce net migration. We will reform the points-based immigration system so that it is fair and properly managed, with appropriate restrictions on visas, and by linking immigration and skills policy. Labour will not tolerate employers or recruitment agencies abusing the visa system. And we will not stand for breaches of employment law. Employers who flout the rules will be barred from hiring workers from abroad. Labour will bring joined-up thinking, ensuring that migration to address skills shortages triggers a plan to upskill workers and improve working conditions in the UK. We will strengthen the Migration Advisory Committee, and establish a framework for joint working with skills bodies across the UK, the Industrial Strategy Council and the Department for Work and Pensions. We will end the long-term reliance on overseas workers in some parts of the economy by bringing in workforce and training plans for sectors such as health and social care, and construction. The days of a sector languishing endlessly on immigration shortage lists with no action to train up workers will come to an end.

bearing_set.reason: The policy directly targets labour-market conditions: it bars employers who abuse visa rules or flout employment law, links immigration to skills/workforce planning, and aims to end sector reliance on overseas shortage-list workers — all with real wage and job-quality effects for domestic workers.

The NHS and social-care sector are among the largest users of overseas worker visas and shortage-list routes; tightening the points-based system and ending automatic shortage-list recruitment will materially affect health and care workforce supply, with direct implications for waiting times and care access.
Explicit linkage to skills policy and mandatory workforce/training plans for overseas-reliant sectors targets FE, skills funding, and apprenticeship starts as the intended domestic-supply mechanism.

Social care is among the sectors most reliant on overseas workers; the same workforce-restriction mechanism could reduce care access and increase waiting times for older people, directly moving the social-care-access indicator.

Mainstream economic evidence (OBR, academic literature) finds net migration supports aggregate output and productivity; restricting it reduces near-term labour supply in key sectors, with a plausible non-negligible drag on real living standards and business capacity.

membership_note: Four fundamentals are warranted: the policy directly targets labour-market protections (O4) and domestic skills development (O7) by design, while generating a non-negligible cross-outcome tradeoff through healthcare staffing (O3) and aggregate economic capacity (O13). Cost-of-living price pass-through (O2) and inequality effects (O14) are plausible but too diffuse and second-order to clear the non-negligible threshold independently.
